newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK COURT ALLOWS REFERENDUM THIS WEEKEND.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK COURT ALLOWS REFERENDUM THIS WEEKEND.

text.p: Referendums on Slovak NATO membership and direct presidential elections will go ahead this weekend despite doubts cast by a Constitutional Court ruling, the central referendum commitee said on Wednesday.

Slovakia's Constitutional Court on Wednesday said the referendum on direct presidential elections was legal, but then cast the plebiscite in doubt by ruling that an appendix to the question was irrelevant and contrary to the constitution.
"The question of whether or not the constitution can be changed by a referendum is valid," spokeswoman Mariana Mochnacova told Reuters from the court's seat in Kosice, eastern Slovakia.

But the court said the text of a draft version of the constitution concerning direct presidential elections, added as an appendix to the referendum question by President Michal Kovac, was unconstitutional.
Still the committee in charge of the vote said the plebescite would go ahead.

"The committee stands by the original questions, as it is unable to change a presidential decision," Pavel Baxa, a member of the referendum commission consisting of all parliamentary parties, told Reuters.
In Friday and Saturday polls, Slovakia is to decide whether the president should be elected directly instead of by a weighted majority in parliament as is currently the case.
The vote will take place alongside a separate referendum on whether Slovakia should join NATO. The common date for both referendums was set by Kovac.

The question on presidential elections, on ballots which are already being distributed, asks: "Do you agree that the president is to be elected directly by the citizens according to the attached draft of the constitutional law?"
The referendum on direct presidential elections resulted from a petition drive by opposition parties. Kovac and the opposition have urged Slovaks to approve both referendums.

The political referendum is seen as an attempt to prevent Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar from possibly assuming presidential powers when the term of Kovac, an avowed foe of the premier, ends next March.

With the present composition of parliament, neither the ruling coalition nor the opposition would be able to muster the two-thirds majority to have their candidate elected. In those circumstances, Meciar would assume presidential powers until a parliamentary election later in the year.

Meciar and allies in his three-party cabinet have strongly opposed the presidential referendum, saying it would illegaly change the constitution. Last week the Slovak Constitutional Court rejected a government motion to declare it illegal.

Interior Minister Gustav Krajci, however on Wednesday announced that he had ordered the printing and distribution of new ballot papers with only the NATO referendum question which Baxa said was illegal and would not distribute any other.
"The minister can print anything he likes but these papers are in no way legal ballots without an official stamp of the referendum committee," Baxa said.

"If Krajci decides to distribute only ballots with the NATO questions without the presidential one, we will have no other alternative than to proclaim the entire referendum as invalid," Kalman Petocz a member of the referendum committee said.
Results of the two votes are expected on Sunday.
